To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Ca current recorded from the chick ciliary nerve terminal is resistant to voltage-dependent Ca current inactivation, has a fast time course, is blocked by Cd and omega-conotoxin, and may be the Ca current involved in transmitter release.

a Ca channel in a cholinergic nerve terminal is similar to the N-type channel in its voltage dependence and pharmacology and that the Ca channel is not subject to inactivation by repetitive depolarization.
a CaN-PT Ca channel was identified and characterized in a vertebrate presynaptic nerve-terminal preparation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of calcium ions in synaptic transmission at the vertebrate neuromuscular junction and in other synapses.
the role of calcium in neurotransmitter release at a vertebrate cholinegic synapse.
the role of calcium in the regulation of synaptic transmission.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CaN-PT channel is a Ca2+ current that activates at about +30 mV and deactivates at -80 m V with time constants of about 1 and 0.5 m s, respectively.

the CaN-PT channel is a Ca2+ channel with the following features: (1) it has a high affinity for Cd2+ and omega-conotoxin, and is therefore classified as an N-type channel; (2) it is not voltage dependent inactivated; and (3) it is located in the calyx presynaptic terminal of the chick ciliary neuron.

the Ca channel in chick presynaptic nerve terminals has a fast time course of activation and inactivation and is resistant to voltage-dependent and Ca-dependent inactivation, but is blocked by Cd and by omega-conotoxin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CaN-PT channel is the most important channel for transmitter release at the vertebrate cholinerge synapse.
CaN-PT is a novel Ca channel subtype that is expressed in presynaptic terminals of vertebrate fast-transmission synapses.
we have identified a novel Ca channel in a presynaptic terminal of the chick ciliary neuron.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the calcium channel in the presynaptic terminal is different than the calcium channel in postsynaptic terminals.
we have shown that the presynaptic nerve terminals have calcium channels that are different from those found on the cell bodies of the neurons.
the Ca channel that is responsible for the fast component of transmitter release is the same Ca channel that is present in the presynaptic terminal.
